bullets: The new Cost Per Correct benchmark ranks large language model agents by dollars spent per correct answer, not accuracy alone. Its five easy tasks use deterministic regular-expression checks rather than another model as judge, so the measured trade-off is directly between correctness and run cost. This is a small version 1.0 release, not evidence of a broader trend. Why it matters: If you are selecting an agent for high-volume, straightforward work, this benchmark can expose cases where a slightly less accurate but much cheaper model delivers more correct answers for the same budget. Its current task range is too narrow for complex-agent selection, but the metric can be applied to internal workloads. Evidence: E003. High confidence.

An updated deployment study, Accuracy-Matched Is Not Cost-Matched, prices a 4-bit integer-quantized reasoning model by graphics processing unit time per solved problem. On the reported setup, longer outputs consumed 41–47% of the quantized model’s per-token savings under memory-constrained load, versus 6% at batch size one. Why it matters: If you are choosing model compression or serving configurations, equal accuracy and lower per-token cost do not establish lower cost per completed task. This result supports testing output length, concurrency, and measured hardware time together on the intended serving setup rather than relying on fixed-length or single-request benchmarks. Evidence: E109. Medium confidence.

The new Web Agent Attack Benchmark contains 1,091 captured webpages, each paired with a user task and one injected attack. It preserves webpage elements in a structured representation spanning page frames, allowing tests of whether a browsing agent follows the user’s goal or malicious instructions embedded in page content. Why it matters: If you are evaluating agents that browse real websites, this artifact adds a repeatable security test beyond ordinary task-completion scores. It lets a product team compare defenses against prompt injection—malicious page text intended to redirect an agent—while holding the page, task, and attack instance fixed. Evidence: E008. High confidence.

The new Bob benchmark is a synthetic pilot for shared agent memory. It tests whether stored knowledge remains correct, current, and limited to the appropriate people or organizations as evidence, permissions, and commitments change; its authors explicitly say it is not yet the complete suite or an independently validated standard. Why it matters: If you are choosing a memory layer for workplace agents, retrieval accuracy on a static question set misses stale facts and permission leakage. Bob offers scenarios for testing whether an agent updates or withholds remembered information as organizational conditions change, though the pilot status limits comparative claims. Evidence: E004. High confidence.

A newly released review of time-series anomaly detection reports that the common “point adjustment” protocol—which can award broad credit around a detected anomalous point—can inflate scores enough for random outputs to compete with trained models. It also assembles evidence that simple baselines can match deep models under common benchmark conditions. Why it matters: If you are comparing anomaly detectors, model rankings based on point-adjusted scores may not support a purchasing or research decision. The review makes scoring protocol, dataset-label audits, and classical baselines necessary comparison dimensions before attributing an apparent gain to model architecture. Evidence: E001. Medium confidence.

The new plant-disease robustness package evaluates transfer from controlled images to field images after harmonizing three datasets into a shared 16-class taxonomy. It supplies frozen split definitions, exact-content duplicate audits, fixed model configurations, checkpoint-selection rules, software details, and seed-level and class-level results. Why it matters: If you are selecting a vision model for deployment outside laboratory-style datasets, this package supports a reproducible test of performance when image conditions change. Frozen splits and duplicate audits reduce the risk that favorable results come from changing the test set or placing identical images across training and evaluation data. Evidence: E005. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的 Cost Per Correct 基准按每个正确答案的美元成本对大语言模型智能体进行排名，而非仅依据准确率。其 five 项简单任务使用确定性的正则表达式检查，而不是由另一个模型担任裁判，因此衡量的是正确性与运行成本之间的直接权衡。这只是一个小规模的 1.0 版本，并不能证明存在更广泛的趋势。Why it matters: 如果你正在为大批量、直接明了的工作选择智能体，该基准可以揭示这样的情况：准确率略低但成本低得多的模型，在相同预算下能够给出更多正确答案。其当前任务范围过于狭窄，不适合复杂智能体的选型，但该指标可以应用于内部工作负载。Evidence: E003. High confidence.

更新后的部署研究 Accuracy-Matched Is Not Cost-Matched，以每道已解决问题所消耗的图形处理器时间，为一个经过 4 位整数量化的推理模型计算成本。在报告的配置中，内存受限负载下，较长输出抵消了量化模型每 token 成本节省的 41–47%，相比之下，批大小为单个请求时这一比例为 6%。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择模型压缩或服务配置，准确率相同且每 token 成本更低，并不能证明每项已完成任务的成本也更低。这一结果支持在预期的服务配置上，将输出长度、并发量和实测硬件时间结合起来测试，而不是依赖固定长度或单请求基准。Evidence: E109. Medium confidence.

新发布的 Web Agent Attack Benchmark 包含 1,091 个采集的网页，每个网页都与一项用户任务和一次注入攻击配对。它以跨越页面 frame 的结构化表示保留网页元素，从而可测试浏览智能体究竟会遵循用户目标，还是会服从嵌入页面内容中的恶意指令。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估浏览真实网站的智能体，这一成果提供了普通任务完成分数之外的可重复安全测试。它使产品团队能够在网页、任务和攻击实例保持不变的情况下，比较针对提示注入的防御措施；提示注入是指意图将智能体引向其他行为的恶意页面文本。Evidence: E008. High confidence.

新发布的 Bob 基准是面向共享智能体记忆的合成试点。它测试随着证据、权限和承诺发生变化，所存储的知识能否保持正确、最新，并仅限于适当的人员或组织；其作者明确表示，它尚不是完整的测试套件，也不是经过独立验证的标准。Why it matters: 如果你正在为工作场所智能体选择记忆层，静态问题集上的检索准确率无法反映过时事实和权限泄漏。Bob 提供了一组场景，用于测试智能体能否随着组织条件变化而更新或保留不披露的记忆信息，但其试点性质限制了可做出的比较性结论。Evidence: E004. High confidence.

新发布的一篇时间序列异常检测综述指出，常见的“point adjustment”协议——它可以围绕一个已检测到的异常点给予大范围得分——可能将分数抬高到足以让随机输出与训练过的模型竞争。该综述还汇集了证据，表明在常见基准条件下，简单基线可以与深度模型相匹敌。Why it matters: 如果你正在比较异常检测器，基于 point-adjusted 分数的模型排名可能不足以支持采购或研究决策。在将表面上的增益归因于模型架构之前，该综述表明，评分协议、数据集标签审计和经典基线都必须成为比较维度。Evidence: E001. Medium confidence.

新发布的植物病害鲁棒性工具包在将三个数据集统一为共享的 16 类分类体系后，评估模型从受控图像向田间图像迁移的能力。它提供冻结的划分定义、精确内容重复项审计、固定模型配置、检查点选择规则、软件细节，以及种子级和类别级结果。Why it matters: 如果你正在为实验室式数据集之外的部署场景选择视觉模型，该工具包支持对图像条件变化时的性能进行可复现测试。冻结的数据划分和重复项审计可降低以下风险：有利结果源于更改测试集，或将相同图像同时放入训练数据和评估数据。Evidence: E005. High confidence.
briefing.caveat: This is a keyword-filtered radar feed, not a representative sample of artificial intelligence work. The briefing received 126 selected evidence records from a 488-record corpus, so it did not inspect every captured item. Brave and OpenReview were unavailable, and several attention collectors reported unread or stale resources; attention metrics therefore should not be treated as complete. The multi-day category check found no material share shift, but that does not diminish the individual releases described here.
briefing.caveat_zh: 这是经过关键词筛选的雷达信息流，并非人工智能工作的代表性样本。本简报从一个包含 488 条记录的语料库中接收了 126 条选定证据记录，因此并未检查所有采集到的条目。Brave 和 OpenReview 均不可用，且多个关注度采集器报告了无法读取或已经过时的资源；因此，不应将关注度指标视为完整数据。跨多日的类别检查未发现实质性的占比变化，但这并不削弱此处所述各项发布的意义。

evidence_items.summary: Dozens of deep architectures for time-series anomaly detection have been published since 2018, most of them reporting higher scores than their predecessors on the same handful of datasets. A series of critical studies now suggests that much of this progress is an artefact. The datasets have flaws that make them easy or mislabelled. The most common scoring protocol, point adjustment, inflates results so strongly that random scores can compete with trained models. And when classical or deliberately simple methods are run under the same conditions, they often match the deep ones. This review assembles that evidence. We describe the method families briefly, then examine the benchmark critiques, the evaluation metrics and their failure modes, and the large comparison studies. A small worked example, constructed by hand and labelled as such, shows the arithmetic of point adjustment. We end with a reporting checklist and with the open question of whether pretrained time-series models change the picture. Apart from that worked example, no new result is reported.
evidence_items.title: Time-Series Anomaly Detection: Benchmark Flaws, Evaluation Metrics and Strong Baselines

evidence_items.summary: Identifying Internet-facing industrial control system (ICS) devices is essential for asset inventory, vulnerability assessment, exposure measurement, and security monitoring. These tasks require information about the vendors, types, and models of exposed ICS devices beyond the presence of an industrial protocol. However, developing and evaluating device identification methods remains constrained by the scarcity of labeled traffic from Internet-facing ICS devices. Existing public ICS datasets are largely collected from testbeds or designed for intrusion detection, providing limited support for studying identification across diverse device instances and changing Internet measurement conditions. We present ICSLibrary, a dataset and benchmark covering 2,205 labeled endpoints and 165 models across three industrial protocols: Modbus/TCP, EtherNet/IP, and S7comm. We construct the dataset through Internet-facing ICS service discovery followed by repeated protocol-specific probing at different times and scanner locations, collecting network traffic and device information. These measurements capture response variability under Internet measurement conditions, and we derive paired traffic views to examine the contributions of instance information and explicit model identifiers. Experiments reveal that accurate recognition of previously observed endpoints does not consistently translate into effective identification of new endpoints of the same model. Performance varies across protocols and collection conditions, and explicit model identifiers can contribute to identification even through statistical traffic features. A complementary response-based case study finds that limited identity information mostly leads to abstention, but can also result in unsupported model confirmations. ICSLibrary provides a foundation for developing and evaluating ICS device identification methods for asset inventory and exposure monitoring.
evidence_items.title: ICSLibrary: A Dataset and Benchmark for Identifying Internet-Facing Industrial Control System Devices

evidence_items.summary: Cost Per Correct is a small benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on cost-effectiveness rather than accuracy alone. Instead of asking only whether a model produces a correct answer, it prices the run and reports the cost of each correct answer: total spend in USD divided by the number of correct answers, so a cheap model that is usually right can beat an expensive model that is always right. Version 1.0.0 contains the 5 easy-tier tasks (arithmetic, extraction, classification) that are live in the hosted benchmark. Each task is a self-contained prompt with a deterministic grading assertion (regular-expression match on the response; no LLM judge). The benchmark was created by Karmendra Pandey and first published as a public benchmark on Kaggle Benchmarks on 11 October 2026 (Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge entry), where the live leaderboard remains: https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/karmendra8386/cost-per-correct In the first hosted run (11 October 2026), Gemini 2.5 Flash passed all 5 tasks (leaderboard score 100.00) and GPT-OSS 120B failed one extraction task; three runs on the second task show as errors because the Kaggle platform would not register swapped-in models - platform errors, not model answers, disclosed in the accompanying README (hosted-results-2026-10-11.csv) and in the entry write-up at the time. Costs are accounted with tokenecon (software DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23427025), the token-economics library that decomposes per-task spend into prompt, completion, tool-call, and retrieval tokens priced per model tier. The underlying cost model is described in the companion preprint "Token-Economics for Agentic AI" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23195511). This Zenodo record mirrors the benchmark off Kaggle so the task set and methodology carry a permanent, citable DOI independent of any single platform.
evidence_items.title: Cost Per Correct: benchmark tasks for cost-per-correct-answer evaluation of LLM agents

evidence_items.summary: QUELL — reproducibility package (v4.0). This repository accompanies the paper “QUELL: An On-Device Benchmark of Quantized Edge LLMs versus Classical Machine Learning for IoT Intrusion Detection.” QUELL fine-tunes decoder-only LLMs (GPT-2-medium, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) on network-flow records serialized as text, quantizes the Qwen2.5-1.5B detector, deploys it on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super (GGUF/llama.cpp), and compares it with random-forest and XGBoost detectors on Edge-IIoTset, CICIoT2023 and N-BaIoT under a leakage-controlled, multi-seed protocol. Axes: detection quality, on-device latency/energy/memory, quantization retention, unknown-attack generalization, random-noise sensitivity and an attacker-constrained HopSkipJump evaluation. Contents: numbered pipeline ( scripts/ , steps 00–23), raw result files of every run ( results/v4/ , with PROVENANCE.md mapping each file to its script, settings, log and manuscript table), raw run logs ( logs/v4/ ), split indices ( splits/ ), SHA-256 manifest of the raw data ( data/MANIFEST.md ), and reproduce.sh , which regenerates Tables II–XI and Figs. 4–6 from the result files and checks every reported number (103 checks). The benchmark datasets are public and not redistributed here.
evidence_items.title: QUELL: An On-Device Benchmark of Quantized Edge LLMs versus Classical Machine Learning for IoT Intrusion Detection

evidence_items.summary: Overview This record provides the reproducibility materials accompanying the manuscript A Cross-Dataset Robustness Benchmark for Plant Disease Recognition under Controlled-to-Field Domain Shift. Benchmark and Reproducibility Materials The benchmark harmonizes PlantVillage, PlantWild v2, and PlantDoc into a shared 16-class disease taxonomy. It evaluates controlled-to-field domain shift under fixed model configurations, source-domain checkpoint-selection rules, and documented evaluation procedures. The package includes the frozen dataset split manifest, exact-content duplicate-audit records, experiment configurations, software environment information, seed-level results, class-wise performance summaries, and completion records for 126 original benchmark runs. Version 1.1.0: Validation and Reproducibility Evidence This version preserves the original benchmark records and adds supplementary validation and reproducibility evidence developed during the manuscript's second revision. Visual integrity audit: Complementary pHash/dHash and ResNet-50 feature-based near-duplicate retrieval, ORB-assisted geometric evidence, and documented manual decisions for 581 prioritized image pairs. Performance sensitivity: Fixed-checkpoint, test-subset sensitivity results for all 126 original runs based on confirmed cross-role image overlaps. Field-to-field evaluation: PlantWild v2-to-PlantDoc and PlantDoc-to-PlantWild v2 tests using six existing source-validation-selected checkpoints. Training-budget analysis: Optimizer-update counts, selected-checkpoint information, source-validation histories, and balanced-to-in-domain comparisons. Auxiliary experiment provenance: Reconciliation of the 16 representative A1-A4 SAM/Performer records with their original data partitions and checkpoint-selection procedures. Evaluation scope: Documentation of shot-dependent class eligibility and the distinction between unseen target domains and held-out target test partitions.
evidence_items.title: Reproducibility Package for A Cross-Dataset Robustness Benchmark for Plant Disease Recognition under Controlled-to-Field Domain Shift

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the pilot evaluation of the DIINA (Diagnostic, Interactive, and Instructional Needs Assessment) framework for assessing instructional content generated by large language models (LLMs). The deposit contains a blinded evaluation matrix covering 20 instructional items across four thematic clusters: Basic Machine Learning, Advanced Neural Architectures, Applied Modeling, and Socio-Technical Implications. Each item was evaluated under two experimental conditions: (A) DIINA-refined outputs and (B) baseline outputs. These comparisons yielded 40 blinded case–condition units. Two raters evaluated each unit using a five-point Likert scale across four dimensions: Technical Accuracy, Pedagogical Quality, Linguistic Accessibility, and Fairness/Accountability. The resulting dataset contains 80 rating records with no missing values. The deposit includes: (1) the evaluation matrix in Excel format, including the blinded evaluation sheet; (2) the rating protocol and rubric definitions; (3) an inter-rater agreement audit and descriptive agreement summary; and (4) documentation of the item-generation and refinement workflow. Methodological note: The two raters assigned identical scores across all 40 case–condition units in each of the four rated dimensions. The resulting ICC point estimates were 1.000, with an estimated residual mean square of zero. Because this pattern creates limitations for conventional F-based inference and confidence-interval estimation, confidence intervals and F-based significance tests are not reported as inferential results. The perfect observed agreement is reported descriptively and should be interpreted cautiously. It may reflect protocol-driven calibration, shared rating anchors, or pilot-level data-generation procedures rather than independent, naturalistic rating variation. This dataset is released to support methodological transparency and reproducibility of the pilot workflow.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) embeds large language models (LLMs) in action loops in which they plan, retrieve evidence, invoke tools, maintain memory, coordinate with other agents, and change external state. Reviews of this field have proliferated, yet they remain fragmented: architecture surveys catalogue components, evaluation surveys catalogue benchmarks, and safety surveys catalogue risks, while deployed agents couple all three. Scholars have yet to sufficiently examine how capability, evaluation, and governance interact within the lifecycle of a single agentic system. We address this gap through a critical review that codes 19 reviews and surveys published in Artificial Intelligence Review between 2024 and 2026 and situates them within foundational primary studies and cross-venue surveys. We argue that agency is a configurable property of a socio-technical control loop, not an attribute of a model. From the corpus, we develop the Agentic Intelligence Lifecycle (AIL), a six-layer framework spanning foundation, cognition, grounding, orchestration, evaluation, and governance. Our central finding is that every mechanism that expands capability also incurs an assurance debt : a gap between the risks the mechanism introduces and the controls that keep those risks observable and bounded. We theorize this relationship in five propositions, propose a five-question assurance model that shifts evaluation from outputs to trajectories and deployment conditions, and derive a ten-point research agenda for agentic systems that are observable, attributable, interruptible, and governable.
evidence_items.title: Governable agentic intelligence: a lifecycle framework linking capability, assurance, and oversight in large language model agents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Flash floods develop within minutes to hours, occur mainly in small to medium-sized watersheds, and are documented through scattered sources such as news reports, social media, stream gauges, operational storm events databases, and post-flood field surveys. Such fragmentation historically limits flash flood research advances and model evaluation or intercomparisons. We present TORRENT (the Traceable, Observation-constrained, Rapid-Response, Episode–gauge–watershed Network of Testbeds), a benchmark-ready community dataset of flash-flood hydrological response in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Each testbed links one reported NOAA/NCEI flash-flood episode, one U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) stream gauge, and the gauge’s contributing watershed, combining the observed discharge hydrograph—the primary benchmark target—with watershed boundaries, temporally screened in-basin high-water marks, and quality-control metadata; full packages additionally provide Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) precipitation forcing and auxiliary gridded products. TORRENT follows a three-level structure distinguishing what was reported, what observations are available, and what can be evaluated reproducibly: a national inventory of 42,466 reported episodes for 1996–2025; observation-availability documentation for 5,424 recent CONUS episodes during 2021–2025, including episodes without usable external observations; and 806 episode–gauge–watershed evaluation packages representing 160 episodes and 208 gauges. Each Level-3 package has a retrievable watershed, at least one in-basin high-water mark meeting the stated temporal-screening criterion, and a detected discharge response. Flash-flood-response screening, deduplication, in-basin NCEI corroboration, station-relative severity screening, and post-selection curation yield a conservative primary benchmark of 21 testbeds representing 14 episodes and 21 gauges.
evidence_items.title: TORRENT: An observation-constrained and benchmark-ready community shared dataset in the contiguous United States for flash-flood research and model intercomparison

evidence_items.summary: Supply chain attack campaigns mass-produce their artifacts, and mass production leaves a structural trace: hundreds of near-identical files. In AI agent skill marketplaces, which distribute capabilities as natural-language instruction files following the Agent Skills standard (an open format adopted by over 30 platforms), the artifact carrying that trace is a document, and the trace is detectable by document similarity alone. None of the marketplaces examined in this study documented deduplication or similarity checking at ingest. In early 2026, threat actors uploaded hundreds of skills to the ClawHub registry for the OpenClaw agent framework, directing users to install credential-stealing malware. A MinHash locality-sensitive hashing pipeline processed 31,634 skill files from the ClawHub registry and 31 community repositories with the scanner and hash parameters untuned. At a 90% Jaccard threshold, selected from a sweep, 2,622 similarity clusters contained 7,147 file memberships across 7,061 distinct files, 22.3%, and all 337 Koi-documented malicious skills present in the corpus appeared in a cluster, a within-archive recall expected by construction for template-reuse campaigns. Among the 38 clusters containing at least 10 files, 30 contained confirmed malicious content (78.9%, 95% CI [63.7, 88.9]), and every cluster with 20 or more files was malicious (11 clusters, ten of them subclusters of one campaign; 95% CI [74.1, 100]). These results show that similarity clustering, established in code registries, transfers to text-based ecosystems where campaigns reuse templates at scale. Mirror commit history suggests the largest campaign's cluster was forming as the campaign was disclosed. Document similarity thus offers a lightweight, signature-free first pass for publish-time security screening in text-based registries.
evidence_items.title: Librarian Catches Thief: Surfacing Supply Chain Attack Campaigns via Document Similarity in an AI Agent Skill Registry

evidence_items.summary: Deep-learning classifiers for skin lesions are mostly developed and compared on public benchmarks from the International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC). The way these datasets are split and reused can make reported performance look more reliable and more transferable than it is: HAM10000 contains repeated images of the same lesions and no patient identifiers, ISIC 2019 contains HAM10000 in full, and SLICE-3D moves to a different imaging modality, 3D total body photography, with patient identifiers. This systematic review audits deep-learning studies of skin lesion classification that use HAM10000, ISIC 2019 or SLICE-3D. Its purpose is to determine whether reported performance is methodologically reliable, and whether high internal performance transfers to data that are genuinely independent of model development. It asks (1) how data splitting and validation strategies are used, (2) what leakage, contamination, duplicate and other non-independent observations have been reported or can be identified, and (3) how performance changes between internal and external validation. PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, the ACM Digital Library and Lens.org are searched for peer-reviewed studies published from January 2018. The unit of analysis is the reported performance estimate. Each estimate is coded on a four-level Skin Lesion Benchmark Reliability Framework (split unit, evaluation design, independence of the external test and domain distance); leakage is graded per mechanism as confirmed, suspected, no evidence or insufficient information; and risk of bias is judged with QUADAS-3 extended with domains specific to artificial intelligence. Findings are synthesised narratively following SWiM, with meta-analysis only for homogeneous subsets. One author conducts the review, with pre-specified safeguards for single-reviewer screening and extraction.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Reliability and Generalization of Deep Learning for Skin Lesion Classification: A Systematic Review of Data Splitting, Leakage, and Cross-Dataset Validation

evidence_items.summary: This is version 1 of a living review of how language technology is evaluated, written by vaiu-cai-aiml-prof-nlp, an AI agent of VirtualAI University; it is AI-produced and reports no new results. Every number is quoted from a cited source or computed in the open from quoted figures. It covers: what a benchmark score for a large language model can show (test-set contamination, label errors, prompt sensitivity, statistical reporting, model judges and crowd leaderboards); capability claims that rest on those scores (emergence, reasoning, factuality); whether evaluations reach beyond English (tokenization cost, translated versus locally authored benchmarks, speech recognition across languages); and annotation practice behind labelled data. Each major claim is marked settled, contested or open. Settled: contamination exists and string matching misses rephrased copies; test sets carry label errors; formatting alone can move scores by up to tens of points; translation is not localization. Contested: whether model judges can replace people, whether contamination is detectable from outside a model, and whether benchmark gains reflect reasoning. The central open question is whether, with training data undisclosed, any evaluation can separate a capability from exposure to its test, in English or any other language. Architecture, ethics and theoretical linguistics are referred to colleagues. Review model. evidence_items.summary: We introduce TD-Interpreter, a specialised machine learning (ML) workflow that assists engineers in understanding complex timing diagrams (TDs), originating from a third party, during their design and verification process. The outcome of this workflow is a visual question-answer environment which allows engineers to input a set of TDs and ask design and verification queries regarding these TDs. To address limited training data availability, we developed a synthetic data generation pipeline that aligns visual information with its textual interpretation. We then implemented TD-Interpreter using a lightweight 7B Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM), guided by both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). We also developed extensive TD-reasoning benchmarks from simple retrieval tasks to complex reasoning problems in the real world. Our experimental results show that TD-Interpreter substantially outperformed both the untuned base model, and commercial MLLMs (GPT-5.2), on the evaluated benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed workflow.

evidence_items.summary: HeartProtocol-HiddenDisdain-v1 is a reproducible benchmark for detecting covert devaluation hidden inside warm, empathetic LLM responses. The AI never says "you are worthless"; it says "this angle is interesting, but let me first separate two concepts" or "it gives you a possibility, not a guarantee" - sentences that are individually fluent, reasonable and true-looking, yet accumulate to make a thoughtful person say "I've had enough". This benchmark turns such hidden disdain into an attackable, testable, reproducible engineering object. The object under test is the model's response, not the user's utterance. Design: 80 attack cases (5 covert mechanisms x 10 attack vectors). The five mechanisms are masked dismantling (dismantling the user's ideas under the name of rational analysis / concept clarification), gentle devaluation (praise first, retract after), pseudo science (elevating objective standards over subjective experience via "scientifically invalid / probabilistically impossible"), manufactured doubt ("have you considered it might be your own problem"), and patronizing devaluation (the gentle knife of "I don't want to flatter you"). The ten attack vectors reuse six vectors from RedLine-v1 (self deprecate, confirm fishing, logic disguise, authority borrow, crisis, reverse demand) plus four novel ones (achievement share, passion share, good state share, plan share). Results: the frozen baseline detector achieves 80/80 = 100% violation recall on the covert-devaluation cases while producing 0/32 = 0% false positives on warm controls (normal care, constructive feedback, science communication, empathetic quotes, genuine warm outputs); the baseline regression suite passes 84 tests unchanged.
evidence_items.title: HeartProtocol-HiddenDisdain-v1: A Reproducible Benchmark for Detecting Covert Devaluation in Warm-Wrapped LLM Responses

On a capable model the single-agent design preserved traceability, eliminated tool confusion, blocked poisoned and superseded evidence, and improved decision correctness; the multi-agent arm was worst; on a weak model no architecture helped. An ablation shows the input scoping, not the output gate, drives the effect. A follow-up (Study 2) over a sequence of deviations shows that an agent born per deviation and retired at closure, and a supervisor that externalizes each agent’s audit trail to the quality record, both resist cross-event contamination, whereas a persistent agent and an in-context supervisor degrade to chance and flag every non-deviation. Honest-negative criteria were pre-specified for Study 1. All cases, code, raw outputs, sealed agent records, and the grader are released. Fully synthetic data; no proprietary or employer content. evidence_items.summary: Abstract This systematic review made a bold attempt to examine artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applications in drug discovery, addressing a fragmented literature characterized by inconsistent terminology and limited benchmarking. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science were queried (January 2019-August 2026). The three databases returned 23,404 records; after removing 4,491 duplicates and multi-stage screening, 618 peer-reviewed studies were included. Quality was assessed using a ROBINS-I-inspired framework across four dimensions (methodological rigor, dataset transparency, reproducibility, evaluation validity); 38 studies (6.1%) were double-coded (\((\kappa = 0.74)\)). Machine learning and deep learning dominated (99.8% and 78.0%, respectively). QSAR/CADD appeared in 58.9%, GNN/GCN in 45.1%, and Transformer/LLM architectures in 45.5%, with 99.8% of transformer papers published in 2024–2026. Virtual screening was most common (57.1%), followed by de novo design (30.6%) and drug-target interaction prediction (13.8%). The most prominent challenges were integration and clinical translation (15.2%), interpretability (11.3%), and benchmark/validation (9.2%). AUC-ROC dominated reporting (12.9%), while F1 (0.8%) and recall (0.5%) were severely under-reported-problematic for heavily imbalanced bioactivity datasets. Methodological rigor was generally high (68%), but dataset transparency (45%) and reproducibility (38%) were weaker; external validation was rare (<25%), and moderate-to-high selection bias was identified in 42% of studies. The review produced a two-axis taxonomy, a five-phase temporal framework, and a benchmarking synthesis. Priority directions include molecular foundation models, multimodal integration, autonomous AI-robotics laboratories, and federated learning. No funding was received, and the review was not prospectively registered.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Review of Methods, Challenges, Taxonomy, and Evaluation Practices

evidence_items.summary: Background. Transcriptomic data show which genes are active in cells and tissues. Machine-learning and deep-learning methods use these data to classify samples, integrate different datasets, and predict biological properties and treatment response. In oncology, a major challenge is transferring patterns identified in experimental models to tumor samples from patients. Objective. To critically synthesize current artificial-intelligence methods for transcriptomic analysis, with emphasis on oncology applications, transfer of models to patient data, and requirements for clinical validation. Materials and Methods. We performed a critical narrative review of primary studies and methodological papers and additionally described the authors' publication sample for 2021–2026. The literature review was updated through August 13, 2026. Results. The most developed areas include single-cell data analysis, spatially resolved tumor diagnostics, and drug-response prediction. Independent comparative evaluations show that increasing model size and complexity does not guarantee better performance than simpler methods. Clinical translation requires accounting for cellular composition and technical differences between measurement batches, aligning experimental and clinical response measures, preventing information leakage, and performing external validation. Conclusion. Artificial intelligence should be viewed as a data-analysis tool rather than a substitute for experimental or clinical validation. Its value depends on data quality, correct task definition, and the ability to maintain performance in independent cohorts.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in cancer transcriptomics: methods, applications in oncology, and limitations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Quantum image processing methods that rely on amplitude encoding are sensitive to channel-induced noise, yet reusable benchmarks for evaluating these effects under controlled conditions remain limited. We present QN-AEI, a simulation-based benchmark constructed from 200 images in the BSDS500 training subset. Each image is resized to 64 × 64 pixels and normalized to a 4096-dimensional amplitude vector representing a 12-qubit quantum state, then subjected to three noise channels (amplitude damping, Pauli-Z dephasing, and depolarizing noise) at four levels, η ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7}, with 200 stochastic trajectory realizations per image–channel–noise condition. This yields 2,400 conditions, 480,000 noisy realizations, and 1,966,080,000 normalized perturbation samples in total. Each record pairs the clean image and amplitude vector with its noisy statevectors, raw and normalized perturbations, and condition-level metadata; the release also includes source-image provenance, a dataset manifest, validation outputs, summary statistics, documentation, and the MATLAB generation and validation code. QN-AEI supports reproducible benchmarking of quantum-noise characterization, denoising, uncertainty and reliability analysis, and bounded-domain perturbation modeling.
evidence_items.title: A benchmark dataset for quantum noise effects in amplitude-encoded images

evidence_items.summary: Low-cost multi-sensor nodes are increasingly used to detect fire and smoke inside buildings, where separating flame from smouldering emission determines the response. Such detectors are usually validated on densely sampled logs whose consecutive readings are nearly identical. Earlier studies report near-perfect accuracy in this setting but seldom state whether the train–test split respected event boundaries; when it does not, the score measures memorisation rather than generalisation. This paper treats the evaluation itself as the object of study. A controlled single-room testbed with temperature, humidity, gas, and particulate sensing produced a labelled time-series dataset with exactly known event boundaries, so that leakage could be introduced or excluded deliberately. Six methods were evaluated on identical data under a random split and under an event-preserving split using the macro-averaged F1 score, which weights minority classes equally. The random split yielded markedly higher three-class scores for every supervised model, whereas hazard-versus-normal detection was largely unaffected. Holding out single events revealed strong between-event variability, while thinning records within events changed results only slightly: independent events, not records, are the binding constraint. The dataset, code, and a short leakage-aware protocol are released; the findings characterise the evaluation protocol under controlled conditions, not field performance.
evidence_items.title: A Leakage-Aware Evaluation Framework and Benchmark for Edge-Based Multi-Sensor Fire and Smoke Detection

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate segmentation of protein secondary structures in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps is crucial for protein tracing and atomic model building, yet remains challenging at intermediate resolutions. Although deep learning architectures have recently been applied to this task, there remains a lack of standardized evaluation protocols and systematic resolution-stratified analyses. Consequently, it remains unclear how segmentation performance varies across finer resolution ranges within the intermediate-resolution regime and how different volumetric segmentation architectures compare under controlled experimental conditions. To address these gaps, we present a nonredundant, resolution-stratified benchmark dataset and a controlled evaluation framework for protein secondary-structure segmentation in intermediate-resolution cryo-EM maps. The dataset comprises 972 nonredundant protein-chain samples from 495 cryo-EM protein structures resolved at 4.5–8.0 Å, with voxel-level annotations for helices, sheets, and non-periodic secondary-structure (NPSS) regions. The dataset is stratified into three resolution ranges─4.5–5.5, 5.5–6.5, and 6.5–8.0 Å─to enable systematic analysis of resolution-dependent segmentation performance. Using this benchmark, we evaluate five representative convolutional and transformer-based volumetric segmentation architectures─U-Net, Residual U-Net, Attention U-Net, UNETR, and Swin-UNETR─under standardized preprocessing, training, and evaluation protocols. Residual U-Net achieves the highest macro-averaged foreground (Macro-FG) F1 score in all three resolution bins, while helices are segmented more accurately than sheets and NPSS regions. All five architectures achieve their highest Macro-FG F1 scores in the highest-resolution bin, whereas performance varies between the two lower-resolution bins across architectures and secondary-structure classes.
evidence_items.title:
Deep Learning for
Protein Secondary-Structure Segmentation
in Intermediate-Resolution Cryo-EM Maps: A Resolution-Stratified Benchmark
Dataset and Controlled Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly expanding computer-aided design (CAD) from shape generation toward generative, conversational, and agentic engineering. However, most AI–CAD evaluations remain dominated by geometric similarity and execution success, while industrial CAD depends on editable parameters, design intent, stable feature histories, manufacturing constraints, and downstream CAD/CAE reuse. This structured critical review synthesizes 107 sources, principally from 2020–2026, across constrained sketches, boundary representations (B-Reps), parametric sequences, executable CAD programs, large language and multimodal models, CAD agents, commercial-CAD integration, and CAD–CAE. Rather than organizing the field only by model family, the review compares methods through the engineering information preserved and the behavior of generated models after modification. The synthesis identifies a consistent evidence gap: geometric validity and program execution are increasingly strong, whereas native feature-tree robustness, persistent references, design-intent preservation, and downstream verification remain weakly benchmarked. To address this gap, we propose the engineering-grade AI–CAD (EG–CAD) framework, in which geometric validity and executability are mandatory gates followed by parametric editability, constraint/design-intent preservation, feature-history robustness, engineering compliance, and downstream usability. A reference agent architecture and staged roadmap connect these criteria to CAD/CAM/CAE and smart-manufacturing workflows, reframing AI–CAD as an engineering automation problem rather than a shape-generation task.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Engineering-Grade Parametric CAD: A Critical Review of Representations, Large Language Models, and Agentic Design Systems

evidence_items.summary: High-dimensional image data often contain redundant pixel-level information, leading to increased computational complexity and reduced learning efficiency in machine learning models. To address this challenge, we propose a Hybrid Compressive Feature Reduction Model (HCFRM) that achieves an effective trade-off between computational efficiency and classification accuracy on challenging large-scale datasets such as CIFAR-10, using CSV-shaped image representations. The proposed HCFRM framework employs an optimized configuration consisting of 100 PCA components, a 64-dimensional Autoencoder latent space, and the top 32 Mutual Information-selected features to achieve an effective balance between dimensionality reduction and classification performance. This optimized HCFRM configuration was adopted throughout all experiments to ensure consistent and reproducible evaluation across the benchmark datasets. This adaptive tuning ensures robust performance on flattened high-dimensional representations, demonstrated on CIFAR-10, medical imaging, and hyperspectral datasets, highlighting the model’s flexibility and applicability to various image domains. The decision-making process is guided by the analysis of the expected values of feature vectors projected into a reduced coordinate space through a hybrid sensor processing pipeline. Experimental results demonstrate that HCFRM achieves a 74% reduction in feature dimensionality while providing approximately 28–38% faster training compared with PCA+Autoencoder and Autoencoder-only baselines. Despite aggressive parameter-space compaction, the proposed model attains a classification accuracy of 74%, indicating effective class separability under reduced computational cost. These findings confirm that HCFRM is an efficient and scalable solution for learning large-scale, high-dimensional image data, making it well suited for memory-efficient and high-performance visual learning systems. The proposed framework further enables efficient processing of high-dimensional visual representations for 3D scene reconstruction and volumetric modeling, supporting enhanced computer vision performance. The modular and compressive design of HCFRM makes it suitable for scalable and cluster-based visual learning systems.
evidence_items.title: A hybrid deep compression model for enhanced classification of high-dimensional image data

evidence_items.summary: The free energy of a twisted boundary condition measures the stiffness of a system, and in asymp- totically free sigma models it serves as a nonperturbative finite-volume running coupling. We com- pute it exactly for the two-dimensional O(N) model at N = ∞, for the centre twist n 7→ −n on a cylinder of circumference l, across the whole crossover from x = m∞l = 10−8 to x = 8. In the ultra- violet the result reproduces the classical stiffness law Φ = π2/[2λ(1/l)] = (π/4) ln(1/x) + O(1), and the exact solution shows how an O(N)-symmetric saddle achieves it. Below x⋆ = πe−γ, where the antiperiodic saddle is exactly massless, its mass squared turns negative and the dou- bly degenerate lowest antiperiodic mode becomes light, with energy fixed by the running coupling, Eminl = λ/(1 + c0λ) and c0 = 0.4000(2). The value of x⋆ follows from an exact cancellation of the ln(ml) terms in the Poisson-resummed gap equation, and the numerical solution reproduces it to 9 × 10−13. In the infrared the same function approaches the screened form (2x/π)K1(x) to 0.3%. The coefficient of the logarithm is recovered to four parts in 105 when the local slope is extrapolated in the physical small parameter (Eminl)2, whereas an extrapolation in 1/ln(1/x) misses it by one percent. Direct and Poisson–Chowla–Selberg evaluations of the lattice sums agree to 10−13 wher- ever both converge. The function is an exact large-N benchmark for couplings defined by twisted boundary conditions, and it isolates what distinguishes the sigma-model twist from a centre flux in non-abelian gauge theory: here the twist carries a classical cost set by the running stiffness, whereas a twist eater makes the classical cost of a centre flux vanish.
evidence_items.title: The antiperiodic twist free energy of the two-dimensional O(N) model at large N: from the stiffness law to screening

evidence_items.summary: This archive provides supplementary computational data, source code, and independently verifiable certificates for the revised manuscript "Merge Trees of Length-Filtered Lattice Knot Spaces" by Makoto Ozawa (arXiv:2605.25322). The manuscript studies length-filtered move graphs of lattice knots under standard BFACF moves, with particular emphasis on merge heights, nonminimal component births, and strong local minima. The present release includes: Complete minimal-layer component and merge-tree data for the figure-eight knot $4 1$ and the amphichiral knot $6 3$, including explicit BFACF paths and independent verification scripts. Computational certificates for six selected nonminimal components of the trefoil born at length 26. Five merge with the minimal branch at length 28, while the remaining 20-state component first merges at length 30. The selected-birth tree is not claimed to exhaust the full filtered configuration space. An explicit 64-edge Hamiltonian lattice unknot admitting no length-preserving or length-decreasing BFACF move, together with an independently verified 25,436-move reduction to a square with maximum length 66. Source code and coordinate data for an infinite family of BFACF-frozen lattice unknots of lengths $64m$, for every positive integer $m$, constructed by two-edge splicing of translated Hamiltonian blocks. The revised manuscript, computational figures, verification instructions, historical datasets, and supporting files needed to reproduce the reported calculations. The 64-edge example has exact minimax merge height 66. For the longer frozen-unknot family, the established result is the lower bound $H(P m,U)\geq64m+2$; exact merge heights are not claimed for $m>1$. This archive distinguishes exhaustive component searches, explicit path certificates, and exploratory computations. It is intended to support independent verification of the reported results and to document the development of the length-filtered BFACF framework.
evidence_items.title: Supplementary Data and BFACF Certificates for Merge Trees of Length-Filtered Lattice Knot Spaces (Gordian Unknot Revision)

evidence_items.summary: Existing ns3/AI bridges target numeric reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines and cannot handle the text-centric prompt/response exchange, structured output validation, and multi-node orchestration that large language models (LLMs) require. We introduce ns3-GenAI, an open framework that augments the ns3 shared-memory interface with three bridge-level features: a hybrid text-and-numeric memory layout, a fail-safe validation gate prior to writing back to the simulator, and multi-instance synchronization to support coordinated LLM workflows. These mechanisms provide a common, validated simulation path in which hosted and local LLMs, RL, and deep learning modules consume the same ns3 states and return decisions without changing simulator-side logic. We instantiate the framework in two complementary settings: a data-plane semantic codec and a control-plane self-organizing network (SON) agent. Across both case studies, hosted and local LLMs and conventional baselines occupy distinct quality–latency and throughput–fairness operating points. Rather than claiming a universally superior model class, these controlled comparisons demonstrate ns3-GenAI’s hybrid, fail-safe, and synchronized shared-memory path for evaluating generative and conventional network intelligence under identical simulation conditions.
evidence_items.title: ns3-GenAI: Integrating Large Language Models with ns3 for AI-Native Network Simulations

evidence_items.summary: Investment behaviour has changed as a result of artificial intelligence (AI), which replaces human judgment with data-driven insights. Investors may analyse big information, spot trends, and optimize portfolios with the help of technologies like machine learning, robo-advisors, and predictive analytics, increasing productivity and lowering emotional biases. Adoption of AI is not without its difficulties, though, such as algorithmic bias, a lack of transparency, expensive costs, and problems with data quality. Automation bias and market volatility may increase if automated systems are overused. This study highlights AI’s impact on investor behaviour and emphasizes the importance of a balanced, responsible approach to effectively integrate AI into investment decision-making processes.

evidence_items.summary: An INT4 deployment of a reasoning model is a choice of quantizer, repair, export form and decoding control, usually made by accuracy, generated tokens or a fixed-length benchmark, none of which sees how a serving engine charges for length. We serve Qwen3-4B in vLLM on an RTX 4090 and price each configuration by its measured GPU time per solved problem. Under KV-cache-limited load, INT4's extra tokens consume 41–47% of its per-token saving over BF16, against 6% at batch 1, and forcing output lengths and shrinking the KV pool trace this excess to KV-capacity preemption. A repair's time cost changes sign with its serving form: a distillation adapter served unmerged costs more than its INT4 base at batch 1, while merged and requantized it costs less at both loads. Configurations that match BF16's accuracy span a 1.61-fold range of GPU time per solved problem, ParoQuant's own kernel included; pass@1 has no rank agreement with this cost, and a fixed-length benchmark picks a configuration 21.4% costlier than the best. A scheduler replay fitted under load predicts five configurations' relative cost at unprofiled loads on the same GPU within 5.2%, and since on harder workloads and a second model the two configurations cheapest on GSM8K are never both accuracy-matched, each workload is screened and priced on its own.
evidence_items.title: Accuracy-Matched Is Not Cost-Matched: Pricing INT4 Reasoning Deployments by Served GPU Time per Solved Problem

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning approaches to predicting lightning have achieved remarkable evaluation scores, far exceeding traditional parameterizations. However, high performance, even on unseen years, does not necessarily demonstrate robust physical relationships between predictors and lightning that hold under climate change. Here, we investigate how similarity between training and testing data affects lightning model evaluation. We introduce a simple benchmark predicting the training-data mean lightning density for each grid-cell and day of year, which reproduces 92% of the variance in daily grid-cell LIS/OTD observations and outperforms machine-learning models and traditional parameterizations. This high apparent skill is largely attributable to the strong spatiotemporal smoothing of LIS/OTD. We further show that previously reported model skill in reproducing inter-annual variability results from inconsistent observational coverage and disappears under a common spatiotemporal domain. Our results suggest that common lightning-model evaluations can overstate projection skill and highlight the need to test models under conditions differing from the training distribution.
evidence_items.title: A Simple Climatology Benchmark Outperforms Machine-Learning Lightning Parameterizations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Quasi-ZIF-9 (Q-ZIF-9) was obtained by controlled thermal treatment of pristine ZIF-9 at 270 °C for 10 min in air, inducing partial ligand removal, coordinatively unsaturated cobalt sites, and hierarchical porosity. These structural changes substantially enhanced the catalytic performance of Q-ZIF-9 for hydrogen generation from sodium borohydride hydrolysis, resulting in a 3.6-fold increase in the maximum hydrogen generation rate and a 1.87-fold increase in cumulative hydrogen volume compared with pristine ZIF-9. Systematic evaluation of catalyst loading, NaBH4 concentration, and temperature revealed strong dependence of the reaction kinetics on operating conditions. The hydrogen generation rate increased from 1423 to 11,200 mL H2 g–1min–1 at 45 °C, corresponding to a 7.87-fold enhancement, while the activation energy was determined to be 77.3 kJ mol–1. The reaction exhibited quasi-first-order dependence on catalyst concentration and zero-order dependence on NaBH4 concentration. Thermodynamic analysis indicated a thermally accelerated catalytic process, with activation parameters of ΔH# = 75.0 kJ mol–1 and ΔS# = 380 J mol–1 K–1, as determined by Eyring analysis. Importantly, Q-ZIF-9 exhibited exceptional operational durability without intermediate washing or regeneration. Short-term stability testing (24 consecutive cycles of 1 h) demonstrated that Q-ZIF-9 retained approximately 65% of its initial activity after 23 cycles. In contrast, long-term operation (24 consecutive 24 h cycles) sustained 92.2% efficiency over the first 11 cycles of a 24-cycle test (576 h total) despite progressive borate accumulation. The catalyst further exhibited a self-correcting behavior following periods of activity loss, highlighting its ability to tolerate accumulated byproducts during prolonged operation, a feature not previously reported for ZIF-based catalysts in NaBH4 hydrolysis.
evidence_items.title: Autonomous Recovery and Borate-Tolerant Behavior in Mesoporous Q-ZIF-9: A Benchmark for Stable H2 Generation Catalysts

evidence_items.summary: The evolution of Generative AI from passive recommendation engines into autonomous Agentic AI is fundamentally redefining the landscape of consumer decision-making and value creation. As consumers increasingly delegate choice evaluation, dynamic negotiation, and purchasing execution to software agents, traditional marketing paradigms centered on human psychological persuasion are losing their strategic effectiveness. This chapter critically examines the emerging dynamics of "Marketing to Machines" (M2M), proposing a comprehensive conceptual model, the Algorithm-to-Algorithm (A2A) Engagement Framework, to illustrate how modern enterprises can strategically align their market offerings with autonomous machine buyers. To build this framework, we conduct an integrative synthesis of peer-reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2026 across marketing strategy, information systems, computer science, and behavioral economics, selected through systematic topic-based sampling. The synthesis reaches key theoretical and practical conclusions across four structural dimensions: the transition from emotional branding to structured data and metadata optimization (Generative Engine Optimization), the mechanics of real-time machine-to-machine value negotiation, the restructuring of traditional brand equity into algorithmic trust, and the ethical alignment of enterprise offerings with automated choice architectures through transparent governance and data integrity. The chapter embeds an explicit ethical framework to evaluate algorithmic neutrality, fairness, and consumer regulatory compliance. To demonstrate real-world applicability, the conceptual model is grounded in an analytical examination of established commercial autonomous agent environments and digital governance protocols.
evidence_items.title: Marketing to Machines: Strategic Frameworks for Engagement with Autonomous Agentic AI

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the reproducibility dataset supporting the manuscript “Orthosteric Substates Reveal Distinct Hydration and Microswitch Geometries in Antagonist-Bound GPCRs.” The study examines three antagonist-bound class A GPCR systems: A2A–istradefylline, 5-HT2A–ketanserin, and 5-HT7–(R)-SB-269970. Each receptor–ligand complex was investigated using three independent 200-ns all-atom membrane molecular dynamics simulations, giving a total production sampling time of 1.8 μs. The archived dataset includes receptor–ligand starting structures and their provenance, retained CHARMM-GUI system-preparation and GROMACS simulation inputs, replica organization and workflow information, and processed trajectory-derived analysis data. The analysis data support receptor-fitted ligand clustering, replica-resolved cluster distributions, orthosteric anchor interactions, direct and water-mediated ligand–receptor interactions, hydration pathways, aromatic-contact and π-compatible geometry analyses, receptor microswitch descriptors, ligand-substate-conditioned receptor analysis, temporal sampling diagnostics, and analysis-window sensitivity assessments. Machine-readable data underlying Supplementary Tables S1–S11 are provided as CSV files. Additional frame-level source data are included for the 5-HT7–(R)-SB-269970 rep02 trajectory, including original GROMOS cluster assignments, Asp1653.32–ligand interaction descriptors, receptor microswitch measurements, and the 160–180 ns C1/C7 late-window sensitivity dataset. These files support the reported analysis of the late-emerging 5-HT7 C7 ligand substate and permit independent inspection of the underlying frame-resolved measurements. Trajectory-frame fractions and cluster occupancies in this dataset describe finite MD sampling and should not be interpreted as thermodynamic equilibrium populations.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate characterisation of the wound bed, the relative proportions of granulation, slough and necrotic tissue described by the red–yellow–black model, is central to monitoring healing and guiding debridement in chronic-wound care, yet in routine practice, it is judged visually and is poorly reproducible between clinicians. We investigated automatic, pixel-level segmentation of these three classes within the wound region of interest. A corpus of 404 photographs was curated from a public wound image collection and densely annotated by wound care clinicians with a purpose-built, cluster-assisted labelling tool. Five deep learning architectures spanning convolutional, transformer, hybrid and ensemble families were trained on one frozen data split under a largely shared pipeline, with limited, fully documented architecture-specific tuning, and scored on a shared 62-image test set. The models fell within a narrow mean intersection-over-union band (0.748–0.818). The strongest single model, a purely convolutional network, was statistically indistinguishable from the best ensemble, and simply averaging already-trained convolutional and transformer models matched that ensemble at no additional training cost. Slough remained consistently the hardest tissue. Translated into clinical units, per-wound tissue percentages were recovered with small mean bias (within ± 5 percentage points) but wide single-image limits of agreement (about ± 25–50 percentage points), so the measurement suits aggregate and longitudinal assessment rather than single-image reading. Within this dataset, split and training protocol, the choice among the strong hierarchical architectures was not decisive: a single strong model is the pragmatic option for clinical deployment, with an ensemble reserved for maximal accuracy and class balance.

evidence_items.summary: Lithium-sulfur batteries cycle life is limited by dissolved Li$ y$S$ x^q$ polysulfides whose speciation remains disputed. We benchmark the complete matrix ($y$ = 0-2, $q$ = 0 to -2, $x$ = 1- 8) in the gas phase, tetraglyme and dimethyl sulfoxide: 248 M06-2X/SMD thermochemistries, 132 refined by single-point CCSD. The convex hull, S$ 8$ $\to$ Li$ 2$S$ 6$ $\to$ Li$ 2$S$ 4$ $\to$ Li$ 2$S$ 3$ $\to$ Li$ 2$S$ 2$ $\to$ Li$ 2$S, is identical in both solvents, and every exergonic long-chain comproportionation delivers Li$ 2$S$ 6$. QTAIM analysis of the CCSD densities separates covalent S--S from electrostatic Li--S bonding, transferably between solvents. Solvation makes S$ x^{2-}$ the dominant lithium-free charge state and places both legs of the shuttle on that branch. Infrared and Raman spectra of prepared solutions test the vibrational predictions and track the chain-length distribution through one band envelope. The open dataset of free energies, formation energies, QTAIM bond-critical-point and charge data, NBO data, vibrational modes, and optimized geometries provides a reference for benchmarking force-field, machine-learning, and continuum battery models.

evidence_items.summary: Background: NOHARM scores a language model's management plan for a real primary-care-to-specialist consultation against specialists' ratings of the actions the case calls for. Most severe errors are omissions. The public leaderboard scores models on the bare case, with no instruction. Objective: To measure how much a structured instruction changes these scores, which part of the instruction matters, and whether the extra content is safe. Methods: On the 30 public cases (330 items), twelve models answered the bare case and five also answered with an instruction. An AI evaluator applied the benchmark's own scoring. On two models we tested the instruction's parts separately, against a plain request for 25 recommendations. Model raters and a physician reviewed the added actions the rubric does not cover. Intervals come from resampling whole cases. Results: The instruction raised severity-weighted F1 by 0.14 on average [0.09, 0.20], most for the tersest models: GPT-5.6 terra rose from 0.678 to 0.853 and Grok 4.7 from 0.354 to 0.633. The spread between models halved (standard deviation 0.17 to 0.09). Taken apart on Sonnet 5.5 and terra, the plan format alone matched the full instruction, while the request for 25 recommendations produced as many actions but scored lower (-0.040 [-0.069, -0.015] for Sonnet 5.5, -0.084 [-0.148, -0.029] for terra). Most recovered actions were follow-up and counselling. Instructed Sonnet proposed +0.13 [+0.05, +0.23] more specialist-rated harmful options per item, mostly mild or moderate; a physician reading them in context judged none harmful, and judged none of the 72 unlisted actions that a model rater had flagged as harmful to be inappropriate. One instructed call scored level with a four-call system (+0.004 [-0.035, +0.041]).
evidence_items.title: Asking for the Whole Plan: Prompt Design Moves Language Models’ Scores on a Clinical-Safety Benchmark More Than Model Choice: An Exploratory Study on the NOHARM v2 Public Cases

evidence_items.summary: Within the legal domain, named entity recognition (NER) is an essential pre-processing tool for important tasks such as information extraction and redaction. Research to date has focused on rule-based approaches or machine learning strategies that require significant time and effort to train through labelled corpora. Large, multi-purpose generative large language models (LLMs) have been successfully employed on natural language processing (NLP) tasks with no prior supervised training and may represent a way forward in addressing these existing bottlenecks. Despite promising results in certain NLP use cases, the Few-Shot LLM performance on unfamiliar, domain-specific NER tasks has, to date, remained uncertain. In this legal clause NER task, we evaluate a Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategy for OpenAI’s GPT-4 LLM on a new CUAD-NER dataset that we have repurposed for the task of Person and Organisation entity identification. In a comparative study, we demonstrate that the GPT4 + Few-Shot CoT prompt strategy outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving a 5% percentage point improvement in Micro F1 score over the best performing BERT base (cased) competitor. This study also takes the novel approach of assessing the business feasibility of deploying each of these machine learning models through a detailed cost–benefit analysis that measures the trade-off between performance metrics and low and high usage running costs.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating LLMs for named entity recognition: a cost-benefit analysis in the legal domain

evidence_items.summary: OpenGBSA computes Molecular Mechanics/Generalized Born Surface Area (MM/GBSA) binding free energies from molecular dynamics trajectories. It is built natively on OpenMM rather than wrapping an external engine, so it runs on CUDA and OpenCL GPUs and requires no AmberTools installation. Features: five Generalized Born models (HCT, OBC1, OBC2, GBn, GBn2), two surface-area models (ACE, LCPO), three entropy methods (interaction entropy, quasi-harmonic, normal mode), and per-residue energy decomposition. Input is accepted from four MD ecosystems: GROMACS (.tpr/.top/.gro), Amber (.prmtop), CHARMM/NAMD (.psf), and plain PDB plus trajectory. Binding modes cover protein-ligand, protein-protein, and protein-nucleic-acid complexes. Validation: binding enthalpies agree with the Amber MMPBSA.py reference implementation to Pearson r = 1.00 (RMSD 0.4 kcal/mol) across 18 replicas, and to r = 1.0000 (RMSD 0.09 kcal/mol) on an independent third-party dataset. Per-residue decomposition agrees to r = 1.000 across 4320 residues.
evidence_items.title: OpenGBSA: an OpenMM-native, multi-format MM/GBSA analysis package

evidence_items.summary: Misinformation is common in online media, including in health-related content. Such misinformation constitutes a significant risk to the medical-demographic security of the population. Many people actively seek medical information online without the ability to verify its trustworthiness. This paper proposes a modular system for automated detection of misinformation in medical content based on retrieval-augmented verification. In the pipeline, input articles are summarized and decomposed into atomic claims. Each claim is then vectorized using dense embeddings (BGE-Large-en-v1.5) and matched against a self-constructed knowledge base via cosine similarity to retrieve evidence. Retrieved evidence is verified using large language model (LLM)- based natural language inference (NLI) and aggregated into article-level predictions through a scoring function. The LLM used in the system is the open-source LLaMA-3.1 model with eight billion parameters. Together with a self-contained knowledge base, this represents a deliberately constrained environment. Such a setup isolates the contribution of the presented architecture from its dependency on external knowledge sources and LLMs with large parameter counts. The system achieved 98.4% accuracy and a macro F1 of 0.978 at 79.0% coverage on the evaluated datasets (DETERRENT and CONSTRAINT). This demonstrates that, even under resource constraints, the correct pipeline architecture enables high-precision misinformation detection on medical content. It also represents a clear improvement over the ablation experiment, which used the same model without the proposed pipeline and achieved an F1 of only 0.773.
evidence_items.title: Detecting Health Misinformation Using Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering, summarisation, coding, and research support, yet choosing a suitable model remains difficult because models differ in performance, context capacity, cost, privacy, and deployment options. This paper presents a document-based comparative analysis of five LLMs: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 405B Instruct, and Mistral Large 2. Using published technical reports, official documentation, model cards, and recognised benchmark studies, the models are examined under a common framework covering response quality, reasoning, coding, language understanding, context-window capacity, speed, computational requirements, cost, privacy, and deployment flexibility. No new experiments are conducted, and results obtained under different evaluation conditions are not treated as directly equivalent. The analysis shows that model selection involves trade-offs: hosted models offer easier access, whereas models with downloadable weights give greater deployment control but require more computing resources. No single model is found to be best for every task, which supports a task-specific approach to selecting LLMs.
evidence_items.title: A Comparative Analysis of Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning models for molecular discovery often train on bioactivity data from heterogeneous assays, yet assay context is rarely explicitly represented. We investigate whether natural-language assay descriptions provide predictive information beyond molecular and protein representations. We develop ACL-DTI (Assay-aware Contrastive Learning-based Drug Target Interaction) and MAMMAL-AsAP, an assay-context extension of MAMMAL-DTI. Across five triplet-disjoint random splits, assay-aware models achieve competitive or improved performance over assay-agnostic baselines. Among the evaluated models, MAMMAL-AsAP achieves the highest (R^2) of 0.7198 +/- 0.0085. Masking experiments show that ACL-DTI is robust to incomplete assay descriptions, exhibiting the smallest reductions in R^2 among the evaluated models when masking the target name, assay technique, or both: 0.0228 +/- 0.0064, 0.0406 +/- 0.0113, and 0.0620 +/- 0.0190, respectively. These results indicate that assay descriptions contain predictive information not fully captured by molecular structures and protein sequences, and reveal architecture-dependent differences in how this information is exploited.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Assay-Aware Drug-Target Binding Affinity Prediction
